status: Draft; agent-assisted source check, not qualified clinical review.
scope: Normal topical cosmetic use; no injection/ingestion/microneedling extrapolation. Not a systematic review.

evaluation.title: Before you buy: benefits, risks and the evidence gaps
evaluation.summary: The research inspected does not establish that either finished serum works better or is safer. There is short-term ingredient evidence, documented preservative reactions in other cosmetics, and safety assessments with defined limits. These are reasons to ask better questions, not to declare either formula harmful.

sections.title: Benefits: ingredient evidence is not a product promise
sections.conclusion: A benefit signal exists for Argireline; superiority of either copper serum is not established here.

paragraphs.text: A randomized placebo-controlled Argireline study in 60 Chinese participants reported improvement in eye-area wrinkle measures after four weeks. It did not identify these two retail serums as the tested treatment.

A separate laboratory study on human cadaver and guinea-pig skin found limited penetration of acetyl hexapeptide-8 from its tested emulsion. This was a 24-hour experiment, not a clinical wrinkle trial; it cannot prove these serums work or do not work.

For this purchase, ingredient research is a starting point. We have not established a head-to-head clinical result for NIOD versus The Ordinary. Do not pay extra on the assumption that a more expensive copper serum has proven superior results.

sections.title: Risks: look beyond the peptide
sections.conclusion: Preservative reactions are documented, but their likelihood in these serums is unknown.

paragraphs.text: A 2024 clinical report describes two cases of contact urticaria—hives after skin contact—from phenoxyethanol in other cosmetics. A case report documents a possible reaction, not how frequently it occurs or that either serum caused it.

The EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety concluded that phenoxyethanol is safe as a cosmetic preservative up to 1.0% under its assessment. That is not a guarantee of individual tolerance or an assay of these US products.

The label check below identifies phenoxyethanol in both formulas. If you have a confirmed allergy to it, that is a concrete reason to discuss alternatives with your clinician. Ingredient presence alone cannot diagnose an allergy or establish that one of these products is riskier.

sections.title: Long-term use: a safety assessment has boundaries
sections.conclusion: Neither a short trial nor an ingredient assessment establishes years of safety for these complete formulas.

paragraphs.text: The CIR assessment includes Copper Tripeptide-1 and specified related peptides and concludes safe use under the practices and concentrations it reviewed. Its scope does not automatically cover every copper-named ingredient or either complete serum.

The inspected CIR report notes gaps in reproductive/developmental toxicity and carcinogenicity data for its reviewed group, while still reaching its scoped safe-use conclusion. A missing dataset is not evidence that these products cause those harms.

This review does not establish long-term harm or long-term safety for either finished serum. We have not performed an exhaustive search or a clinical safety review. We also do not transfer injection, ingestion or microneedling findings to normal cosmetic application on intact skin.

sections.title: Value: what would justify paying more?
sections.conclusion: A price premium is not evidence of a health or performance advantage.

paragraphs.text: The inspected studies and safety assessments do not compare the two finished products. They cannot establish that paying more buys better wrinkle reduction, lower allergy risk or greater long-term safety.

Our catalog still lacks a verified price for NIOD’s 30 mL variant, so we cannot calculate a fair cost difference yet. Compare the exact size and current price separately from the scientific evidence. Personal format preferences may matter, but we have not tested texture or wear.

evaluation.labelContext: The current US ingredient lists for both products name Phenoxyethanol and Chlorphenesin. These are additional label checks, not additions to our selected-peptide list. Individual preservative concentrations are not given in the inspected lists. The academic phenoxyethanol case report concerns different cosmetics; it is not an adverse-event report for these two serums. NIOD also advertises product tests with 31–32 people over 4–12 weeks. We have not assessed their full protocols or an independently published head-to-head result; these brand-reported claims are separate from the academic evidence above.

research.supports: An example of ingredient research with a defined population and duration, rather than a test of either compared copper serum.
research.limits: Four weeks in one population. Neither CAIS3 nor The Ordinary’s copper serum is the tested product identified in the abstract. No product winner or long-term safety conclusion follows.
research.commercialContext: The publisher reports no funding and no declared conflicts. These are author declarations, not an independent audit.
research.access: Publisher abstract and acknowledgments inspected; full methods behind subscription were not reviewed.
research.authors: Wang Y, Wang M, Xiao S, Pan P, Li P, Huo J.
research.design: Randomized, placebo-controlled; 60 Chinese participants, 3:1 allocation, four weeks.
research.finding: The abstract reports improved eye-area wrinkle measures with Argireline relative to placebo.
research.integrity: No correction or retraction notice was seen on the inspected publisher page. This is not a comprehensive integrity clearance.
research.publicationTitle: The Anti-Wrinkle Efficacy of Argireline, a Synthetic Hexapeptide, in Chinese Subjects: A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Study

research.supports: Shows that the tested emulsion and skin model matter when interpreting peptide-delivery claims.
research.limits: Not a living-person efficacy or long-term safety trial. Neither retail serum was tested.
research.commercialContext: Authors have an FDA research affiliation. Funding and conflict declarations were not verified from the abstract; affiliation is not FDA product approval.
research.access: PubMed abstract and bibliographic metadata via Europe PMC; full methods not reviewed.
research.authors: Kraeling ME, Zhou W, Wang P, Ogunsola OA.
research.design: 24-hour in vitro diffusion experiment using human cadaver and hairless guinea-pig skin, not a human participant trial.
research.finding: The abstract reports mostly surface-retained peptide and no detected peptide in the dermis under the tested conditions.

research.supports: Documents individual contact-urticaria reactions involving phenoxyethanol in other cosmetics.
research.limits: Two cases cannot estimate incidence, establish the risk of either compared serum, or prove chronic systemic toxicity.
research.commercialContext: Funding and conflict declarations were not verified in the accessible material.
research.access: University repository summary and PubMed/Europe PMC bibliographic metadata; full clinical report not reviewed.
research.authors: Marzola E, Melloni L, Caligiure A, Gianessi F, Bianchi A, Borghi A, Corazza M.
research.design: Two clinical cases involving other cosmetics.
research.finding: The repository summary describes contact urticaria associated with phenoxyethanol, with reactions at the face rather than other tested sites.

research.supports: Provides the EU committee’s 1.0% preservative safety conclusion under its assessed conditions.
research.limits: Not a US product approval, a measurement of either formula, or a guarantee against an individual reaction. The opinion excludes non-cosmetic exposure.
research.commercialContext: European Commission scientific advisory opinion; not published by a retailer.
research.access: Official SCCS conclusion and scope on the European Commission page; the underlying toxicology dossier was not independently reanalysed.

research.supports: Provides a scoped safe-use conclusion for specified peptide identities, practices and concentrations.
research.limits: Does not test these finished products or establish their safety over years. NIOD’s exact label name is not silently equated with a different name in the report.
research.commercialContext: CIR is funded by the Personal Care Products Council and describes its panel/review process as independent. Industry-submitted data are included; this is not a government approval.
research.access: 2014 final CIR report, including scope, data gaps and discussion, plus 2018 journal publication abstract/bibliography. Not a new independent toxicology analysis.
research.authors: Johnson W Jr, Bergfeld WF, Belsito DV, et al.
research.publicationTitle: Safety Assessment of Tripeptide-1, Hexapeptide-12, Their Metal Salts and Fatty Acyl Derivatives, and Palmitoyl Tetrapeptide-7 as Used in Cosmetics
research.design: Expert assessment of specified cosmetic peptide ingredients; underlying final report released June 30, 2014.
research.finding: The panel’s favorable conclusion is conditional on the reviewed uses, concentrations and peptide identities.
